scenes.heading: Cell structure
scenes.sub: Why do mitochondria carry their own DNA?
scenes.say: Why can some antibiotics kill bacteria without harming you? And why do your mitochondria carry their own DNA? The answers are in how cells are built.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A flatmate who moved in with their own bag and never moved out
scenes.science: Mitochondria came from an engulfed bacterium
scenes.breaks: Nobody decided anything: this happened by evolution over an enormous span of time, when a host cell engulfed a bacterium.
scenes.say: Think of a flatmate who arrived carrying their own bag, got wrapped in a box from the house, and never left. That's endosymbiosis. Mitochondria came from a bacterium engulfed by a host cell. Chloroplasts came later, from an engulfed cyanobacterium.

scenes.heading: Evidence for endosymbiosis
scenes.say: Remember: two DNA ribs divide. Both organelles have two membranes, their own circular DNA, and seventy S ribosomes, and they divide like bacteria do. They're also bacteria-sized, and their r R N A sequences place them among bacteria.
scenes.caption: Remember: Two DNA Ribs Divide. Both organelles have two membranes, their own circular DNA, and 70S ribosomes, and they divide like bacteria do. They're also bacteria-sized, and their rRNA sequences place them among bacteria.

scenes.heading: Prokaryotic vs eukaryotic
scenes.say: Pro means no nucleus, eu means do. Prokaryotes have a nucleoid, circular DNA and seventy S ribosomes, with no membrane-bound organelles. Eukaryotes have a nucleus, linear DNA on histones, eighty S ribosomes and many organelles.
scenes.caption: Pro means no nucleus, eu means do. Prokaryotes have a nucleoid, circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, with no membrane-bound organelles. Eukaryotes have a nucleus, linear DNA on histones, 80S ribosomes and many organelles.

scenes.heading: Path of a secreted protein
steps: Folds and is glycosylated in ER
scenes.say: Think of a factory and post office. A ribosome docks on the rough E R, and the protein folds and gets sugars added inside. A vesicle carries it to the Golgi, which labels and sorts it. It leaves from the trans face, and exocytosis releases it from the cell.
scenes.caption: Think of a factory and post office. A ribosome docks on the rough ER, and the protein folds and gets sugars added inside. A vesicle carries it to the Golgi, which labels and sorts it. It leaves from the trans face, and exocytosis releases it from the cell.

scenes.heading: Magnification
scenes.say: Use the I A M triangle: image equals actual size times magnification. So magnification is image size divided by actual size. Always convert to the same units first. One millimetre is one thousand micrometres.
scenes.caption: Use the I AM triangle: Image = Actual size × Magnification. So magnification is image size ÷ actual size. Always convert to the same units first. 1 mm = 1000 µm.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: A mitochondrion is 36 mm long on a TEM image at ×18 000. How long is it really?
scenes.say: A mitochondrion is thirty-six millimetres long on an image magnified eighteen thousand times. Convert: thirty-six thousand micrometres. Divide by eighteen thousand: two point zero micrometres. That's a sensible size for a mitochondrion.
scenes.caption: A mitochondrion is 36 mm long on an image at ×18 000. Convert: 36 000 µm. Divide by 18 000: 2.0 µm. That's a sensible size for a mitochondrion.

scenes.say: Quick recap. Prokaryotes have no nucleus and seventy S ribosomes. Secreted proteins go rough E R, Golgi, then out. Two DNA ribs divide. Magnification is image over actual. And resolution, not magnification, limits detail: about two hundred nanometres for a light microscope. Now try the practice questions!
